suggestions.rationale: Depression is a recognized psychological comorbidity in psoriatic arthritis, and systematic-review evidence reports both appreciable depression prevalence and an elevated risk of incident depression in psoriatic disease populations that include PsA. These population-level findings support condition-specific research of the PsA/depression relationship, but they do not establish that PsA caused or aggravated an individual depressive disorder; the literature also describes probable bidirectionality and substantial heterogeneity.
evidenceGaps: Qualified diagnosis of a depressive disorder rather than symptom-screening results alone
Chronology comparing depressive-disorder onset or worsening with PsA diagnosis, inflammatory activity, pain, functional limitation, and treatment
Documentation of PsA disease burden, including pain, function, skin disease where relevant, and treatment response
Evaluation of alternative psychiatric, medical, medication-related, psychosocial, substance-use, and sleep-related contributors
Qualified rheumatology or mental-health opinion addressing the individual relationship if causation or aggravation is asserted

sourceReferences.citation: Lukmanji et al., Journal of Cutaneous Medicine and Surgery (2021), PMID 33263264
sourceReferences.note: Systematic review and meta-analysis found greater incident depression risk in psoriatic disease and reported that PsA status did not explain the high heterogeneity; the authors also note probable bidirectional effects. Supports a population-level relationship, not an automatic individual nexus.

sourceReferences.citation: Hernández-Rodríguez et al., Rheumatology International (2024), PMID 38797775
sourceReferences.note: Overview of systematic reviews found depression among the commonly reported psychological comorbidities of PsA, with pooled depression prevalence across included reviews of approximately 11.9% to 20%. Supports comorbidity/association and screening relevance, not individual causation.
